new_articles.title: Advances in microglia replacement therapy for neurodegenerative diseases
new_articles.abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a critical pathological basis for a variety of neurodegenerative diseases. Replacing diseased microglia with functionally competent cells offers a potential strategy to restore immune homeostasis in the central nervous system (CNS) and modify disease progression. In recent years, microglia replacement therapy has evolved into a diversified technological framework encompassing cell sources (e.g., bone marrow-derived cells, peripheral blood cells, and stem cell-derived cells), strategies for eliminating resident microglia (e.g., irradiation, chemical ablation, and colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibitors), and delivery routes (systemic or local transplantation). In preclinical models—including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP), Krabbe disease, and mucopolysaccharidoses—this approach has demonstrated potential to clear pathological substrates, improve neurological function, and delay disease progression. In humans, clinical precedent is currently limited to conventional hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-based interventions in selected inherited neurological diseases, whereas advanced replacement protocols remain preclinical. This review systematically summarizes the key technological advances in microglia replacement therapy and its applications in neurodegenerative diseases, and discusses future directions in this rapidly evolving field.

new_articles.title: Why postmortem neuroimaging matters in ALS-FTD: a molecular calibration framework
new_articles.abstract: Postmortem neuroimaging offers a critical molecular calibration framework for ALS-FTD biomarkers by enabling direct integration of in vivo imaging signatures with regional proteinopathy, cellular pathology, and tissue microstructure to improve biological interpretation and therapeutic relevance.

new_articles.title: TREM2c·3G>A promotes aberrant microglial-endothelial signaling, impairs BBB integrity, and enhances Aβ and Tau accumulation
new_articles.abstract: We identified a novel start-codon mutation in TREM2 (TREM2c·3G>A, M1I) that causes complete loss of TREM2 expression and is associated with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD) in humans. This mutation triggers profound blood-brain barrier (BBB) impairment in both humans and mice, positioning BBB impairment as an early trigger rather than a downstream consequence of neurodegeneration in AD. Mechanistically, TREM2 deficiency causes NF-κB-driven upregulation of microglial CCL2, which activates CCR2 on endothelial cells and induces tight junction internalization. The resulting BBB compromise permits the leakage of peripheral pathological proteins, including β2-microglobulin, accelerating amyloid plaque formation and premature Tau pathology. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR2 and endothelial cell-specific Ccr2 knockdown restored BBB function and reduced amyloid plaque burden, highlighting this pathway as a tractable therapeutic target. Our findings establish a direct mechanistic link between microglial dysfunction, BBB breakdown, and pathogenic protein accumulation, thereby redefining the vascular role of TREM2 in neurodegenerative disease.

new_articles.title: Revealing white matter hyperintensities-related faster posterior cortical tau accumulation in Alzheimer’s Disease
new_articles.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is a multifactorial disorder in which cerebrovascular abnormalities frequently co-occur with β-amyloid (Aβ) and tau pathology. White matter hyperintensities (WMH), a common marker of cerebral small vessel disease, are associated with cognitive impairment and are highly prevalent across the AD continuum. However, the extent to which WMH burden is associated with spatial patterns of tau pathology and its longitudinal accumulation remains unclear.MethodsWe examined 1,455 participants with Aβ PET, tau PET, T2-FLAIR MRI, and cognitive assessments from four independent cohorts: ADNI (n = 710), A4/LEARN (n = 440), GHABS (n = 249), and PREVENT-AD (n = 56). Resting-state functional MRI data were available in subsets of ADNI and A4, and CSF SomaScan proteomic data were available in ADNI and PREVENT-AD. Associations of WMH burden with longitudinal tau accumulation and network-based tau propagation were examined. A data-driven approach was used to identify distinct tau subtypes. WMH burden, tau accumulation, and clinical and biological characteristics were evaluated across subtypes.ResultsGreater total WMH burden was associated with faster tau accumulation (ADNI, A4) or higher subsequent tau burden (GHABS) in the temporal meta-ROI among Aβ-positive (A+) individuals. These associations were attenuated after accounting for Aβ burden. However, greater WMH burden, particularly in the occipital lobe, remained significantly associated with faster tau accumulation and network-based tau propagation in occipital regions after adjustment for Aβ burden. An occipital-dominant tau subtype was identified, characterized by greater occipital than parietal tau burden. This subtype showed more widespread associations between WMH and tau accumulation, an older estimated age of Aβ positivity onset, and a higher prevalence of hypertension, together with slower global tau accumulation and cognitive decline than the parietal-dominant subtype. CSF proteomic analyses further identified vascular and extracellular matrix pathways related to tenascin-C (TNC) in the occipital-dominant subtype.ConclusionsGreater WMH burden was associated with faster tau accumulation and network-based tau propagation, with the most consistent associations involving occipital regions. These findings suggest that the association between WMH burden and occipital tau progression may reflect vascular contributions to regional tau vulnerability in the context of AD pathology.

new_articles.title: APOE-driven lipid dysregulation in Alzheimer’s disease: from glia to myelin
new_articles.abstract: The APOE4 allele is the predominant genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and its pathological influence is increasingly understood through the lens of lipid biology. APOE functions as the primary lipoprotein in the central nervous system, coordinating the distribution of cholesterol, phospholipids, and fatty acids among neurons and glial cells to sustain membrane integrity, synaptic function, and myelin maintenance. The E4 isoform carries structural alterations that compromise its lipid carrying capacity and receptor interactions, with consequences that extend across multiple brain cell types. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on how APOE4 disrupts lipid homeostasis in a cell type specific manner, covering astrocytic lipid buffering and oxidative stress responses, microglial phagocytic and lysosomal dysfunction, oligodendrocyte cholesterol handling and myelin biosynthesis, and neuronal lipid clearance. We also address the relationship between APOE isoforms and the hallmark pathologies of AD, including amyloid beta accumulation and tau propagation. Insights from protective natural variants such as APOE2, Christchurch, and Jacksonville are discussed in the context of therapeutic target identification. Evidence drawn from human postmortem studies, neuroimaging, single-cell transcriptomics, and iPSC derived brain cell models converges on a model suggests that disrupted glial lipid metabolism may contribute early in disease, although whether it initiates or amplifies pathology remains unresolved. Targeting APOE-mediated lipid pathways therefore offers a promising and mechanistically grounded avenue for disease modifying intervention in AD.

new_articles.title: REV-ERBα regulates photoreceptor metabolism and visual function and protects against inherited retinal degeneration
new_articles.abstract: The retina is a metabolically demanding tissue essential for visual function. Disruptions in retinal metabolic pathways are linked to degenerative eye diseases like retinitis pigmentosa (RP). In this study, we found that REV-ERBα (Nr1d1), a nuclear receptor central to mitochondrial biogenesis, is critical for retinal metabolism, visual function, and protects against retinal degeneration. Expression of REV-ERBα is present throughout retinal cells, with high levels in photoreceptors. Both systemic genetic deletion and rod photoreceptor specific deletion of REV-ERBα in mice resulted in dampened visual function with reduced amplitude of a- and b-waves in the electroretinogram. REV-ERBα-deficient retinas and photoreceptor cells exhibited impaired mitochondrial function with decreased oxygen consumption and altered expression of metabolic genes. Importantly, activation of REV-ERBα with a synthetic agonist SR9009 substantially delayed photoreceptor loss in an rd10 genetic mouse model of RP, with slower retinal thinning, reduced levels of photoreceptor apoptosis, and partially preserved visual function. Together, our findings position REV-ERBα as a critical regulator of retinal and photoreceptor metabolism and function, and a promising therapeutic target for addressing retinal degeneration. Modulating REV-ERBα activity may offer a novel strategy for protecting retinal neurons and mitigating vision loss in eye diseases like RP.

new_articles.title: The neutral lipidome in Parkinson’s disease
new_articles.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disease with increasing evidence implicating lipid and fatty acid metabolism as important contributors to pathogenesis. Disrupted lipid metabolism, including sphingolipids, ceramides, cardiolipins, cholesterol, phospholipids and others, have been implicated in PD pathological processes, such as alpha-Synuclein (αS) aggregation, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. PD-associated dysregulation of neutral lipid metabolism is emerging as a key contributor to PD-associated lipid dyshomeostasis, prompting investigation of novel PD therapeutic targets and biomarkers in this pathway. However, PD-associated alterations of the human ‘neutral lipidome’ remains poorly understood, motivating this review. Herein, we comprehensively evaluate human studies reporting PD risk loci and concentrations of neutral lipids (triacylglycerols [TAGs], diacylglycerols [DAGs], monoacylglycerols [MAGs]) in samples from individuals with or without PD. Genetic and lipidomic evidence supports a dysregulated neutral lipidome in PD, as indicated by: (i) PD risk loci in or affecting neutral lipid metabolism pathways, (ii) PD-associated differences in neutral lipid concentrations in postmortem brain tissue and biofluids, (iii) meta-analysis-identified association between higher TAG concentrations and lower PD risk, (iv) PD candidate therapeutic targets in neutral lipid pathways, and (v) candidate neutral lipid PD biomarkers. Collectively, these data support the disruption of neutral lipid homeostasis as a contributing mechanism in PD. Thus, we propose the PD-associated neutral lipidome as an underexplored and important axis contributing to PD pathogenesis that can be targeted for the development of PD biomarkers and disease-modifying therapeutics.
